body.heading: Notice the light
paragraphs: A shadow forms where an object blocks light. On a sunny day, a fixed object’s shadow can change as the Sun appears to move across the sky. Looking at the shadow lets you observe the light without looking directly at the Sun.
Use the same object and the same level surface each time. A moving object or a sloping surface can make comparisons harder to interpret.

body.heading: Follow a changing angle
paragraphs: When the Sun is low in the sky, a vertical object often casts a long shadow. As the Sun gets higher, that shadow becomes shorter. Its direction changes as well.
The shortest shadow is around local solar noon, which need not be 12:00 on a clock. Location, season, and the clock system all matter. A cloudy day can make a shadow difficult to see.

body.heading: Keep an observation notebook
paragraphs: Make two or three drawings at different times. Label the time, the weather, and which way the shadow points. Describe what you actually saw before trying to explain it.
Never look directly at the Sun. If you investigate outside, choose a safe place away from roads and use ordinary sun protection. Children should work with an adult.

takeaway: Watch one fixed object at different times. Changing sunlight can change both the length and direction of its shadow.
